blocks.text: For his first book, Unshorn , Dutch photographer Milan Gies sets men who have fallen and risen again in dialogue with horses and the landscapes they share, in a study of vulnerable and endured masculinities.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Milan Gies .

Unshorn feeds on its author’s own life, as he looks to his subjects for an echo of his own frailties. As a child, Milan Gies “wanted to disappear into horses.” The former professional show jumper, born in 1977, was eighteen when he watched a man beat a rearing horse during training. “It rose one last time, high into the air, broke its neck and crashed down at my feet. Foam and blood came from its mouth. […] He left. I stayed.”

Haunted by the animal, the young witness would later seek oblivion in the glare of the footlights, then in the haze of drugs. “I kept mistaking resistance for freedom.” Now based in Amsterdam, he teaches and coaches professional photographers at his own small academy, Studio 307. “The men I photograph exist outside the mainstream of society. They too have lived, struggled, fallen and had to find their way back up.” With a patient eye, he wins their trust until he can lay them bare, body and heart.

Milan Gies captures male flesh under strain, braced, every gesture marked by pain, endurance and survival. In the hush of a pared-back set, a figure beaded with light bends one leg mid-fall, caught between collapse and a dancer’s grace. The stage finds its answer in the riding ring, where a sculptural piebald horse rises in revolt, one foreleg flung into the void. “Every time I feel the reins tighten,” the artist confides, “something inside me starts to rear” — because the world, as he puts it, “rewards the obedient: perform, produce, belong, win, keep moving.” Against that current, the raw-nerved rebel kicks over the traces.
The book closes not on relief, but on a question Milan Gies carries: “I still don’t know whether that horse is the strongest part of me or the part that will eventually kill me.”
Unshorn by Milan Gies is published by Void . 96 pages, limited edition of 750 copies, €50.
